## Data: Lemurs 

::: midi
Today’s data contains a subset of the original Duke Lemur data set available in the [TidyTuesday GitHub repo](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/blob/master/data/2021/2021-08-24/readme.md). This data includes information on lemurs less than 24 months old from three taxa:

- Eulemur rufus (ERUF), commonly known as Red-fronted brown lemur
- Propithecus coquereli (PCOQ), commonly known as Coquerel’s sifaka
- Varecia rubra (VRUB), commonly known as Red ruffed lemur.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
lemurs <- read_csv("data/lemurs-sample-lt24mo.csv")
```

## Variables

**Predictors**:

- `taxon` : Code made as a combination of the lemur’s genus and species. Note that the genus is a broader categorization that includes lemurs from multiple species. (`ERUF`: Eulemur rufus, `PCOQ`: Propithecus coquereli, `VRUB`: Varecia rubra)
- `sex` : Sex of the lemur (`M`: Male, `F`: Female)
- `age`: Age of the lemur when weight was recorded (in months)
- `litter_size`: Total number of infants in the litter the lemur was born into (this includes the observed lemur)

**Response**: `weight`: Weight of the lemur (in grams)

## Response: `weight`

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(lemurs, aes(x = weight)) +
  geom_density(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of weight", 
  subtitle = "Lemurs < 24 months old",
  x = "Weight in grams")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
lemurs |>
  summarise(
    Min = min(weight),
    Median = median(weight),
    Max = max(weight),
    IQR = IQR(weight)
  ) |>
  kable()
```

## Predictors

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| out.width: "100%"
#| fig-align: center


p1 <- ggplot(lemurs, aes(x = taxon)) +
  geom_bar(color = "black", fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Taxon")

p2 <- ggplot(lemurs, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "black", fill = "steelblue", binwidth = 2) +
  labs(title = "", 
       x = "Age in months")

p3 <- ggplot(lemurs, aes(x = litter_size)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "black", fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Litter size")

p1 + p2 / p3
```

## Response vs. predictors

```{r}
#| echo: false
p4 <- ggplot(lemurs, aes(x = taxon, y = weight)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    y = "Weight in grams",
    x = "Taxon"
  )

p5 <- ggplot(lemurs, aes(x = age, y = weight)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    y = NULL,
    x = "Age in months"
  )


p6 <- ggplot(lemurs, aes(x = litter_size, y = weight)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    y = NULL,
    x = "Litter size"
  )

p4 + p5 / p6
```

. . .

**Goal**: Use age, taxon, and litter size to understand variability in the weight of lemurs younger than 24 months old.

. . .

::: question
Why do we want to use a single model versus 3 separate simple linear regression models?
:::

# Multiple linear regression (MLR)

## Multiple linear regression (MLR)

Based on the analysis goals, we will use a **multiple linear regression** model of the following form

$$\begin{aligned}\text{weight} ~ = 
\beta_0 & + \beta_1 ~ \text{age} \\ & + \beta_2 ~ \text{taxon}_1 \\ &+ \beta_3 ~ \text{taxon}_2 \\
&+\beta_4~ \text{litter_size} \\
& +\epsilon
\end{aligned}$$

## Multiple linear regression

**Recall:** The simple linear regression model

$$Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1~ X + \epsilon$$

. . .

The form of the multiple linear regression model is

$$Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_1 +  \dots + \beta_pX_p + \epsilon$$

<br>

. . .

Therefore,

$$E(Y|X_1, \ldots, X_p) = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_1 +  \dots + \beta_pX_p$$

## Fitting the least squares line

Similar to simple linear regression, we want to find estimates for $\beta_0, \beta_1, \ldots, \beta_p$ that minimize

$$\sum_{i=1}^{n}\epsilon_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n[y_i - \hat{y}_i]^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n[y_i - (\beta_0 + \beta_1x_{i1} + \dots + \beta_px_{ip})]^2$$

<br>

. . .

The calculations can be very tedious, especially if $p$ is large

## Matrix form of multiple linear regression

Suppose we have $n$ observations, a quantitative response variable, and $p$ \> 1 predictors
$$\underbrace{
\begin{bmatrix}
y_1 \\
\vdots \\
y_n
\end{bmatrix} }_
{\mathbf{y}} \hspace{3mm}
= 
\hspace{3mm}
\underbrace{
\begin{bmatrix}
1 &x_{11} & \dots & x_{1p}\\
\vdots & \vdots &\ddots & \vdots \\
1 &  x_{n1} & \dots &x_{np}
\end{bmatrix}
}_{\mathbf{X}}
\hspace{2mm}
\underbrace{
\begin{bmatrix}
\beta_0 \\
\beta_1 \\
\vdots \\
\beta_p
\end{bmatrix}
}_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
\hspace{3mm}
+
\hspace{3mm}
\underbrace{
\begin{bmatrix}
\epsilon_1 \\
\vdots\\
\epsilon_n
\end{bmatrix}
}_\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$$

::: question
What are the dimensions of $\mathbf{y}$, $\mathbf{X}$, $\boldsymbol{\beta}$, $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$?
:::

## Matrix form of multiple linear regression

As with simple linear regression, we have

$$\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}$$

. . .

Generalizing the derivations from SLR to $p > 2$, we have

$$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (\mathbf{X}^
 \mathsf{T}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{y}$$

as before.

## Model fit in R

```{r}
#| echo: true

lemur_fit <- lm(weight ~ age + taxon + litter_size,
              data = lemurs)

tidy(lemur_fit) |>
  kable(digits = 3)
```

## Model equation

$$\begin{align}\hat{\text{weight}} = -0.772 &+137.479 \times \text{age}\\
&+ 462.184 \times \text{taxonPCOQ}\\  
&+ 1020.390 \times \text{taxonVRUB}\\
& -14.101 \times \text{litter\_size}
\end{align}$$

::: callout-note
We will talk about why there are only two terms in the model for `taxon` soon!
:::

## Interpreting $\hat{\beta}_j$

- The estimated coefficient $\hat{\beta}_j$ is the expected change in the mean of $Y$ when $X_j$ increases by one unit, <i><b>holding all else constant.</b></i>.

. . .

- **Example:** The estimated coefficient for `age` is 137.479. For each additional month in a young lemur’s age, their weight is expected to be greater by 137.479 grams, on average, holding taxon and litter size constant.

::: callout-note
Alternate interpretation: For each additional month in a young lemur’s age, their weight is expected to be greater by 137.479 grams, on average, adjusting for taxon and litter size.
:::

## Prediction 

::: question
What is the predicted weight for a PCOQ lemur who is 10 months old and was born in a litter with 3 lemurs?
:::

<br>

```{r}
#| echo: true

-0.772 + 137.479  * 10 +462.184 * 1 + 1020.390 * 0 - 14.101 * 3
```

. . .

The predicted weight for this lemur is `r -0.772 + 137.479 * 10 +462.184 * 1 + 1020.390 * 0 - 14.101 * 3` grams.

## Prediction in R {.midi}

Just like with simple linear regression, we can use the `predict()` function in R to calculate the appropriate intervals for our predicted values:

```{r}
#| echo: true

new_lemur <- tibble(
  age  = 10, 
  taxon = "PCOQ", 
  litter_size = 3
)

predict(lemur_fit, new_lemur)
```

## Cautions

- **Do not extrapolate!** Because there are multiple predictor variables, there is the potential to extrapolate in many directions
- The multiple regression model only shows **association, not causality**
  - To show causality, you must have a carefully designed experiment or carefully account for confounding variables in an observational study (causal inference)

# Model comparison

## Model evaluation: RMSE & $R^2$

- **Root mean square error, RMSE**: A measure of the average error (average difference between observed and predicted values of the outcome)

- **R-squared**, $R^2$ : Percentage of variability in the outcome explained by the regression model

## Comparing models  {.small}

Let's consider the following models:

```{r}
#| echo: false

lemur_fit_2 <- lm(weight ~ age + taxon + litter_size + age * taxon,  data = lemurs)

tidy_lemur_fit_2 <- tidy(lemur_fit_2) |>
  select(term, estimate)


tidy(lemur_fit) |>
  select(term, estimate) |>
  right_join(tidy_lemur_fit_2, by = "term") |>
  kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("term", "Model 1", "Model 2"))
```

<br>

<center>**How do we decide which model to choose?**</center>

## Comparing models

::: incremental
- When comparing models, do we prefer the model with the lower or higher RMSE?

- Though we use $R^2$ to assess the model fit, it is generally unreliable for comparing models with different number of predictors. Why?

  - $R^2$ will stay the same or increase as we add more variables to the model.

  - If we only use $R^2$ to choose a best fit model, we will be prone to choose the model with the most predictor variables.
:::

## Adjusted $R^2$

- **Adjusted** $R^2$: measure that includes a penalty for unnecessary predictor variables
- Similar to $R^2$, it is a measure of the amount of variation in the response that is explained by the regression model
- Use the `glance()` function to get $Adj. R^2$ in R

```{r}
glance(lemur_fit)$adj.r.squared
```

## $R^2$ and Adjusted $R^2$

$$R^2 = \frac{SSM}{SST} = 1 - \frac{SSR}{SST}$$

<br>

. . .

$$R^2_{adj} = 1 - \frac{SSR/(n-p-1)}{SST/(n-1)}$$

where

- $n$ is the number of observations used to fit the model

- $p$ is the number of non-intercept terms in the model

## Using $R^2$ and Adjusted $R^2$

- Adjusted $R^2$ can be used as a quick assessment to compare the fit of multiple models; however, it should not be the only assessment
- Use $R^2$ when describing the relationship between the response and predictor variables
